findings.passage: A host who wants everyone at the table is slow to turn anyone away. That accounts for who was in the room.
findings.problem: The quote this rests on ("find humanity in everyone") is moved out of its context. GQ prints it in its closing paragraph as something she said "about her seemingly boundless fervor to pick up the pieces" after the show went wrong. GQ does not present it as a policy on whom she invites. The draft introduces it as "Her stated policy toward difficult people", uses it to explain why people accused of homophobic jokes were in the room, and then states the motive as fact ("That accounts for"). No opened source gives her reason for the guest list, so this is a motive the author supplied.
findings.acceptance_test: The quote appears with GQ's own framing (said about picking up the pieces after the show). Any link between that quote and who she invites is labelled as the profile's inference with its limit, or is removed. No sentence states as fact why she invited or kept anyone unless a source gives her reason.

findings.passage: It does not excuse the jokes to the people they were about, and she has not disputed that criticism.
findings.problem: "She has not disputed that criticism" is not supported, and her actual response is missing. Dexerto (December 9, 2025) says she called "a lot of the criticism" "really valid" without saying which criticism. The same report says she explained that the show is "much bigger than it used to be" and that she has to "adjust for that" in its jokes and bits, and that she defended her own joke about Rakai's ban as understood in the room but not at home. So she partly disputed it, and she never conceded a named charge. The draft also drops GQ's lead-in to the "You're a pedophile!" line ("she said she was working on it"), which changes how that quote reads. The sentence does not separate her own monologue jokes from the cohost's Diddy joke, and the racism and homophobia claims come from unnamed posts that GQ summarises.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage reports what she said on December 8, 2025 as Dexerto reports it: the bigger audience, adjusting the jokes, and her defence of the Rakai joke. It does not say she conceded or left undisputed any specific charge. The "complimentary joke" quote carries GQ's framing that she said she was working on her jokes. Her own jokes are distinguished from the cohost's. The racism and homophobia claims stay attributed to unnamed online posts as relayed by GQ.

findings.passage: The reply to Frost belongs here, and it repeats the Vice interview from nearly three years before. Attacked, she lists what she gave: the dinner, the months, the night.
findings.problem: The two statements are treated as the same move, and they are not the same situation. In Vice the quote follows her saying her family had seen sexual deepfakes of her: "For my 65-year-old dad, it'd be a hard time explaining to him that that's not real…". She was setting her real work against what her family now saw. The draft cuts that lead-in, calls the quote "a list", and makes it the first instance of a habit of itemising what she is owed. That reads a statement about sexual-image abuse as a personality tell, and the parallel carries one of the three reasons the profile gives for Type 2 ("She goes live, and she points to the dinner"). Two related problems: the Type 3 paragraph says "the tears are what an image under attack costs" with no scope, and the tears in this article include the deepfake stream; and the Frost account leaves out that she refused to uninvite him (Dexerto, November 18, 2025: she "shut down any notion of uninviting Frost").
findings.acceptance_test: The Vice quote appears with its context (her family and her father seeing the images). The link between February 2023 and November 2025 is labelled as the profile's inference, the difference between the two situations is stated, and "it repeats" is not asserted as fact. The paragraph giving the three reasons for Type 2 says a response to sexual-image abuse is weak type evidence, or stops relying on it. "The tears" in the Type 3 paragraph is limited to the awards backlash. The Frost account says she did not uninvite him.

findings.passage: What the reporting shows is a grievance about friends aired in public, then a move to shield the same friends from the audience. The critics' point stands: the couple supplied the names.
findings.problem: The draft says the tone of the podcast remarks is unknown, yet calls them a "grievance" and opens the passage with "the pattern ran small". It keeps her two sharpest lines and omits her explanation in the same Dexerto report: "Yes, people were late to our wedding. Yes, it set the wedding back. No, it does not need to be farmed to oblivion by the plague that is drama clippers" and "This job is weird cause you share your personal life online and then as you become more ingrained in it other content creators become your personal life." "The critics' point stands" is an author verdict on a dispute where the critics are unnamed users; the standard asks for no verdict lines. The harshest line quoted ("I hate them until I die") is her husband's, and the research record warns against using the shared wedding as evidence about her.
findings.acceptance_test: Her explanation from the October 22, 2026 posts is quoted or fairly paraphrased beside the lines already used. The critics' argument is reported as theirs with no author ruling on it. No sentence characterises the seriousness or tone of the podcast remarks until the audio is reviewed. "The pattern ran small" is removed or replaced with a plain statement of what this episode can and cannot show. Ahgren's line is not used as evidence about her.

findings.passage: The complaint is not quite fair to them. She is the one who withholds the surname.
findings.problem: This is the author's verdict on her, and it turns the withheld surname into a fault. GQ and the BBC say only that she does not make it public. The record in this same draft includes three swattings, and the BBC interview it cites reports men turning up at her shop looking for her. No opened source gives her reason, so the draft cannot assert one either way, but presenting the withholding as unfairness to friends without that context is a harmful reading. GQ's "hyperbolic" and Valkyrae's irritation already supply the counterpoint. The same remark is then restated as fact where it carries the most weight: the closing line ("By her own count, the people at those tables do not know her last name or her birthday") and the meta_title ("The Host Nobody Knows"), which drops the "says" that the title keeps. In October 2026 she married one of those peers and described other creators as having become her personal life.
findings.acceptance_test: The author's fairness verdict is removed, or replaced by counterpoints attributed to GQ and Valkyrae. The withheld surname is not framed as a failing; if it stays in this passage, the safety record already in the article sits beside it without being claimed as her stated reason. The closing paragraph signals that the remark was hyperbole and was disputed in the room, or uses her directly quoted line instead. The meta_title attributes the claim to her, as the title does.

findings.passage: Her parents were "mostly focused on getting divorced."
findings.problem: Three of her quotes about childhood are stacked so that they imply neglect, and her own qualifier is left out. In the next paragraph of the same GQ profile she says: "My parents definitely weren't neglectful". Her mother died in 2016 and her father is a living private person; neither can answer. The page also never tells the reader in this section that her mother has died; it appears only as an aside in the Type 6 paragraph.
findings.acceptance_test: Her statement that her parents "definitely weren't neglectful" appears beside the childhood quotes. It can be quoted on its own, without the abuse detail that follows it in GQ, which should stay out.

findings.passage: She wants the effort seen and disowns the wish in the same sentence.
findings.problem: This states a private wish as fact from one sentence said in her kitchen. A plainer reading is available: she is saying she feels she has no standing to complain about an awards show. That fits what she told GQ during the same visit: "I'm not trying to farm sympathy, but there is no sympathy."
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence is marked as the profile's reading and the plainer alternative is given beside it, or the sentence is cut.

findings.passage: GQ described that panel as secret, so outsiders cannot check its share.
findings.problem: The body and the FAQ "Were the Streamer Awards rigged?" both end on the doubt (the FAQ: "so outsiders cannot check that share") and never say what the record shows. The reporting opened for this profile (GQ, BBC, Dexerto) presents no evidence of rigging and names no accuser; the evidence record says the same ("No evidence of rigging was found in this research"). "Unproven" alone leaves that out. The FAQ question will sit under her name in search results.
findings.acceptance_test: The body and the FAQ both say that the cited reporting presents no evidence of rigging and that the accusers are unnamed viewers. The panel caveat stays, placed after that statement.

findings.passage: In between she improvised: a rerun channel she set up to fund the 2024 show got both of her Twitch accounts banned for 41 minutes on February 10, 2024, after it showed a clip that broke Twitch's rules
findings.problem: An adverse fact rests on Wikipedia alone; the evidence record says the underlying Game Rant report was not opened. "She improvised" is the draft's characterisation. The reader is not told what the clip was or whether she chose it, so the sentence implies fault the record does not establish. I did not open this source.
findings.acceptance_test: The underlying report is opened and the sentence says what the clip was and who ran the channel; or the sentence is attributed plainly as Wikipedia's account with "improvised" removed; or it is cut.

protected_passages.passage: That is her account, given twice on the record. This profile reports it in her words and draws no conclusion about her personality from it.
protected_passages.reason: The right handling of her abuse disclosure: her words, no causal claim, and none of the further detail GQ prints. Keep this restraint and do not add detail.

protected_passages.passage: Her forgiveness is her own to give and does not change the record of what happened.
protected_passages.reason: Reports her stance on Ewing without vouching for it or judging it, and keeps his conduct on the record.

protected_passages.passage: But the vigilance has a plain outside cause, and anxiety alone does not make a Six.
protected_passages.reason: Credits her circumstances (swatting, deepfakes) before her personality. This is the standard the rest of the page should meet.

protected_passages.passage: QTCinderella goes by Blaire and does not publish her surname.
protected_passages.reason: Respects a privacy line she has drawn. The page prints no surname, no initial and no full birth date; keep it that way.

protected_passages.passage: Nearly all of the evidence about motive is her own account, given to reporters between 2022 and 2025, often in weeks when she was promoting an event or defending one.
protected_passages.reason: States the limit of the record plainly, so the reader knows the typing is a reading of interviews and not knowledge of her.

assessment: I read this as a fairness proxy and do not speak for her. I opened six sources on 2026-11-10 to check the passages with the most potential for harm: GQ, Vice, BBC and the three Dexerto reports (November 18 and December 9, 2025; October 22, 2026). I did not open Inven Global, ET, Polygon, GGRecon, Sportskeeda, THR or Wikipedia, and no stream or podcast audio. The draft is careful in the places that matter most. The childhood abuse disclosure is reported in her words with no causal claim and without GQ's further detail. The deepfake account matches Vice, including Ewing's admission. The rigging accusation is marked unproven with her denial. The page prints no surname and only a birth year, and it has a full section on what the record cannot show. The problems are in the interpretive sentences, where an inference is written as fact or a quote is moved to a context its source does not give. The two worst are the "humanity in everyone" quote used to explain the guest list (subject-01) and "she has not disputed that criticism" (subject-02); both are contradicted by the sources they cite. Next is the use of her statement about her family seeing the deepfakes as the first example of a habit of listing what she is owed (subject-03). Three of her own explanations are missing: her December 8 remarks on the jokes, her October 22 posts on the wedding, and her statement that her parents were not neglectful. Two author verdicts on her ("not quite fair to them", "The critics' point stands") go against the standard's rule on verdict lines. Similarity: both flagged matches against Olivia Dean are a one-line disclaimer and a one-clause definition of Type 2. I compared the arguments. The two profiles share the Type 2 over Type 3 frame at medium confidence, but the evidence and the deciding observations are different, so I raise no finding. Two notes with no finding attached. The keyword "QTCinderella real name" is acceptable only while the page keeps answering it with "Blaire" and nothing more; the wikipedia and same_as links lead to a page that prints her surname initial, which is the owner's call. And as research already noted, the rigging controversy has no named critic, so that part of the controversy standard is still unmet. Risk flags stay as research set them: sensitive allegations and contested typing.
